offence_severity: Life imprisonment under Section 302 IPC and 10 years imprisonment under Section 376 IPC
physical_harm: Injuries including sexual assault, strangulation, and ligature marks on the neck
key_evidence_accepted: The dead body of the deceased was found inside the house of the appellant with blood stains under the cot, blood stains on the bed-sheet and on the floor underneath the cot, and the doctor's post-mortem report indicating sexual assault and strangulation. The appellant's alibi was found to be false.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of the witnesses, particularly the child witness Nitesh (PW.3), and found that the circumstances were consistent with the guilt of the accused, with no reasonable ground for concluding innocence.
post_offence_conduct: The appellant was present in his house when police arrived and his alibi that he had gone to a liquor shop was found to be false.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 24.10.1999; Trial judgment: 19.9.2001; High Court decision: 11.1.2008; Supreme Court decision: 20.9.2011
legal_representation: For the accused: D.N. Goburdhan, Prabal Bagchi, Karitka Sharma, Balendu Shekhar; For the State: Arun R. Pednekar, Sanjay Kharde, ~sha Gopalan Nair
investigation_status: Chargesheet filed under Sections 302 and 376 of the IPC
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction under Sections 302 and 376 IPC, life imprisonment; High Court: Affirmed conviction, enhanced sentence to death penalty; Supreme Court: Set aside death sentence, restored life imprisonment
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant caused the death of a minor girl aged 10 years by strangulating her after committing rape on her. The case was based on circumstantial evidence, and the trial court convicted the appellant and sentenced him to life imprisonment under Section 302 IPC and 10 years imprisonment under Section 376 IPC. The High Court upheld the conviction but enhanced the sentence to death penalty.
defence_argument: The defence argued that there was no evidence on record to connect the appellant with the crime. Circumstantial evidence was not sufficient to indicate the appellant's guilt, and the High Court was not justified in enhancing the punishment from life imprisonment to death sentence.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that a conviction based on circumstantial evidence must be conclusive, exclude all possible hypotheses except the one to be proved, and form a complete chain of evidence. The court also applied the 'rarest of rare cases' test for the imposition of the death sentence.
precedent_relied_upon: Krishnan v. State represented by Inspector of Police (2008) 15 SCC 430; Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra AIR 1984 SC 1622; Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab AIR 1980 SC 898; Machhi Singh & Ors. v. State of Punjab AIR 1983 SC 957; Paramjeet Singh @ Pamma v. State of Uttarakhand AIR 2011 SC 200; Wakkar & Anr. v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2011) 3 SCC 306; Mohd. Mannan @ Abdul Mannan v. State of Bihar (2011) 5 SCC 317; Inspector of Police, Tamil Nadu v. John David (2011) 5 SCC 509; SK. Yusuf v. State of West Bengal AIR 2011 SC 2283; C. Muniappan & Ors. v. State of Tamil Nadu AIR 2010 SC 3718; Rabindra Kumar Pal alias Dara Singh v. Republic of India (2011) 2 SCC 490; Surendra Kofi v. State of UP & Ors. (2011) 4 SCC 80; Sudam@ Rahul Kaniraril Jadhav v. State of Maharashtra (2011) 7 SCC 125
sentencing_rationale: The case does not fall within the 'rarest of rare cases', and the High Court was not justified in enhancing the punishment. The death sentence awarded by the High Court was set aside, and the life imprisonment awarded by the Trial Court was restored.
